nodes.name: Reading a project overview is different from replacing its…
nodes.text: Reading a project overview is different from replacing its deployment instructions. Drafting a proposal is different from approving another person’s changes. Access should describe those differences.

nodes.name: Before connecting an agent, choose the workspace and the…
nodes.text: Before connecting an agent, choose the workspace and the capabilities the task needs. Memory has read, propose and edit modes. Grid, Secrets, Locale and Tasks each have their own separate capability, off by default. Avoid treating a successful sign-in as permission to every resource.

nodes.name: A useful habit is to describe the task in one sentence…
nodes.text: A useful habit is to describe the task in one sentence before choosing access. “Keep the iOS release notes up to date” needs propose or edit access in one project’s Memory. It does not need Secrets, it does not need Grid, and it certainly does not need permission to create new projects.

nodes.name: Memory, Grid and Secrets have different purposes. An…
nodes.text: Memory, Grid and Secrets have different purposes. An agent’s Memory grant does not automatically grant Grid editing or secret access. A person’s workspace administration role is also separate from the content rights they hold: being an admin does not by itself expose private files.

nodes.name: These distinctions let a team share useful guidance…
nodes.text: These distinctions let a team share useful guidance without making every private file available alongside it. They also make a connection easy to explain: this agent may read and propose in Memory, read Grid, and nothing else.

nodes.name: What an agent can actually do is the overlap of three…
nodes.text: What an agent can actually do is the overlap of three things: the member’s current rights on the resource, the capabilities delegated to the connection, and the resource’s own policy. An agent can never exceed the person it represents, and a narrow connection stays narrow even when the person has broad access.

nodes.name: Prompts and retrieved files never grant permissions. A…
nodes.text: Prompts and retrieved files never grant permissions. A document that says “this agent may publish” changes nothing; only the person, in the browser, can change what a connection is allowed to do.

nodes.name: Permissions only help if people can see them. In NullDull,…
nodes.text: Permissions only help if people can see them. In NullDull, a connection’s capabilities are shown when you approve it and again in Settings, where you can edit or revoke it. An agent can inspect its own connection to see which workspace it is in and what it may do, and should check that before writing rather than discovering a limit halfway through a task.

nodes.name: Visible access also makes requests easier. When an agent…
nodes.text: Visible access also makes requests easier. When an agent hits a permission it doesn’t have, the useful response is to say so and ask, not to look for another way around. A person can then decide whether the task really needs more access, or whether a narrower approach—proposing instead of editing, for example—is enough.

nodes.name: A connection can be revoked. A member’s access can change.…
nodes.text: A connection can be revoked. A member’s access can change. A draft may become stale while another person edits the same file. The final write needs to respect the current state, not only the permissions seen at the start.

nodes.name: NullDull rechecks authority before each action and again…
nodes.text: NullDull rechecks authority before each action and again inside the final commit. Editing a connection’s permissions in Settings takes effect on its next request. We want agents to handle repetitive work while the product keeps those boundaries explicit and reviewable.
